Review the definition of syndromic scoliosis.

Explain how to perform an appropriate workup for patients with syndromic scoliosis.

Definition of Syndromic Scoliosis
The most recent definition of syndromic scoliosis, according to the Classification of Early-Onset
Scoliosis, is scoliosis in syndromes for which no known congenital or neuromuscular etiology
exists, but an association with scoliosis is present.1
Syndromic scoliosis may be associated with ligamentous laxity; hypotonia; or nonbony
structural intraspinal abnormalities, such as tethered cord or syrinx. Patients with syndromic
scoliosis are more likely to have kyphosis and are more likely to experience complications than
patients with idiopathic scoliosis1 (Resources 1 and 2).
Nonsurgical Management
Treatment strategies for syndromic scoliosis differ from those for idiopathic scoliosis. Although
older studies recommended bracing, evidence for bracing, particularly in this patient
population, is poor, and bracing may be detrimental in some patients.
Cast immobilization has been performed and is an excellent tactic to delay management;
however, it is associated with a lower likelihood of good outcome in patients who have
syndromic scoliosis compared with patients who have idiopathic scoliosis2,3. (Video 1)

Preoperative Workup
The preoperative workup is based on the underlying etiology; however, a higher likelihood of
cardiac manifestations and intrathecal abnormalities exists in patients with syndromic scoliosis
compared with patients with idiopathic scoliosis.4,5
Surgical Management
A larger percentage of patients with syndromic scoliosis progress to surgical treatment
compared with patients who have idiopathic scoliosis, and patients with syndromic scoliosis
tend to progress to surgical treatment at a younger age. Surgical treatment of these patients is
associated with a higher complication rate, with increased complications related to
comorbidities, blood loss, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leaks, and the need for revision
surgery.6 (Resource 3), (Videos 2 and 3)

Scoliosis may be associated with thoracic kyphosis or minimal rotation7-11
Spinal Manifestations
Tethered spinal cord, syrinx, Chiari malformation, myelomeningocele (if associated with
myelomeningocele, scoliosis is considered congenital/structural)
Tethered Cord
Occurs in 0.05 to 0.25 per 1,000 individuals and has multiple causes
May result in pain, neurologic or urinary dysfunction, and orthopaedic manifestations13
Orthopaedic manifestations in as many as 47% of patients who undergo simple filum
release; these manifestations include lower extremity spasticity, diminished lower extremity
strength, and foot deformity14
Improvement or stabilization of scoliosis may occur in patients who are detethered if their
curves are less than 40° at the time of detethering and if their skeletal maturity is greater
than Risser grade 3 to grade 5.15-17
Syrinx
Abnormal fluid within the spinal cord that can occur spontaneously or in combination with a
tethered cord or Chiari malformation (Figure 1)

Marfan Syndrome
Etiology
Autosomal dominant mutation on the fibrillin-1 gene on chromosome 15q21, causing a
connective tissue disorder that results in increased tissue laxity and an increased risk of
scoliosis, pes planus, and acetabular protrusio (Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man [OMIM]
#154700; (Resource 5)
Preoperative Workup
Cardiac evaluation because of increased risk for aortic root, aortic, or pulmonary artery
dilation; mitral valve prolapse; valvular regurgitation; spontaneous pneumothorax21
Medical Management
Patients may require beta blockers to decrease the risk of aortic dilation.
Diagnosis
Clinical diagnosis is based on the Ghent criteria.22-24
With Negative Family History
Aortic root dilation Z-score of 2 or higher and ectopia lentis
Aortic root dilation Z-score of 2 or higher and mutation of fibrillin-1 gene
Aortic root dilation Z-score of 2 or higher and systemic score of 7 points or higher
Aortic root dilation and ectopia lentis and mutation of fibrillin-1 gene

Spinal Manifestations
Scoliosis develops in more than 60% of patients with Marfan syndrome. Patients have an
earlier mean onset than those with idiopathic scoliosis and are more likely to have double or
triple major curves. Scoliosis is more likely to be progressive compared with idiopathic
scoliosis, with curves greater than 40° at skeletal maturity continuing to progress throughout
life.24-26
Dural ectasia is present in 59% to 100% of patients, which may result in headache, back pain,
spontaneous dural leak, narrowing of the pedicles, vertebral scalloping, and hardware fixation
failure.27-29(Figure 2)

Nonsurgical management
Bracing is less successful in patients with Marfan syndrome than in patients with idiopathic
scoliosis, with only a 17% success rate in preventing surgical treatment compared with a 75%
success rate for idiopathic scoliosis.
May have some benefit for smaller curves (15° to 25°)26
Surgical Management
Typically requires longer constructs than those for idiopathic scoliosis; more likely to require
fusion to the pelvis because of increased rates of pelvic obliquity, junctional curves, distal
degeneration, or dysplastic curves.29-31
Higher complication rate compared with idiopathic scoliosis; increased blood loss, dural tear
(8% to 10%; also can develop later because of dural ectasia or bone erosion), infection (7% to

Loeys-Dietz syndrome
Etiology
Five different mutations are associated with Loeys-Dietz syndrome. The most common is an
autosomal dominant mutation in the transforming growth factor beta signaling pathway on
chromosome 9q22 and is distinguished from Marfan syndrome by hypertelorism and
abnormal uvula or cleft palate (OMIM #609192).
Other causes include an autosomal dominant mutation in transforming growth factor beta
receptor type 2 on chromosome 1q41, which is associated with scoliosis and foot deformities
(OMIM #614816) and an autosomal dominant mutation in transforming growth factor beta-3
on chromosome 14q24, which is associated with skeletal overgrowth, cervical spine
instability, and clubfeet (OMIM #615582). 
Preoperative Workup
Increased risk of vascular aneurysms and higher risk of dissection or rupture than in Marfan
syndrome and vascular tortuosity in the head and neck32
Spontaneous pneumothorax; bowel and uterine ruptures have been reported.32
Spinal Manifestations
Cervical spine instability develops in more than 70% of patients and is associated with
substantial vertebral abnormalities, including midline defects and vertebral body hypoplasia.33
Scoliosis develops in 25% to 70% of patients, develops at a younger age, and is more likely to
progress to surgical management. Patients tend to have more severely dysplastic pedicles.33-
35
Nonsurgical management via bracing is successful in only 4 of 15 patients.34
Dural ectasia, which may result in increased risk of CSF leaks and anterior sacral meningoceles,
is present in 40% to 72% of patients.28,34,36

Cervical spine instability is common and often requires anterior/posterior spine fusion.34
Thoracic scoliosis and thoracolumbar scoliosis are managed differently, depending on patient
age. In younger children, Bressner et al34 reported that the following:
9 of 16 growing rod surgical procedures were associated with rod fractures.
7 of 24 procedures resulted in CSF leaks.
Adding on of deformity was common, with 5 of 11 requiring extension of fusion.
Definitive posterior spine fusion may be complicated, with increased risks of blood loss and
CSF leaks.34
Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome
Etiology
Heterogenous group of connective tissue disorders associated with mild to severe skin laxity,
easy bruising, valvular abnormalities, and joint hypermobility (Resource 5)
Vascular subtype may be associated with vascular, pulmonary, or intestinal ruptures that occur
spontaneously or with minimal trauma.36,37 More than 13 subtypes have been observed;
these subtypes vary in severity and may are associated with autosomal recessive or autosomal
dominant inheritance.38
Hypermobile forms account for more than 90% of case; vascular subtypes account for fewer
than 5% cases.32 All forms are associated with easy bruising, skin laxity, and joint
hypermobility39-44 (Table 1).

Spinal Manifestations
Scoliosis is present in the classic, hypermobile, vascular, spondylodysplastic, and
kyphoscoliotic subtypes.32
The kyphoscoliotic and musculocontractural forms are characterized by severe hypotonia at
birth, early-onset kyphoscoliosis, ligament laxity, and skin fragility..
Medical Management
Patients may require beta blockers to reduce the risk of arterial dilation and vessel rupture.
Patients have an increased risk for vascular complications, including excessive bleeding and
stroke, because of vessel dissections, ruptures, and perforations.
For hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, tailored physical therapy focused on
core/extremity muscle strengthening, proprioception and joint stability is the first line
treatment option.45
• Brace management is more likely to fail in patients with hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos
syndrome than in patients with idiopathic scoliosis.
Surgical Management
Reports of severe blood loss have been described with anterior surgery;46 however,
subsequent studies using the Pediatric National Surgical Quality Improvement Program
database have shown no difference in blood loss between patients with Ehlers-Danlos
syndrome and patients with adult idiopathic scoliosis but have reported a higher rate of
pulmonary embolism (2%) and an unplanned revision surgery rate (7% versus 3%, respectively)
in patients with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.47
An increased risk of neurologic complications may exist because of a combination of
ligamentous laxity and vascular fragility.48

Prader-Willi Syndrome
Etiology
Prader-Willi syndrome is an example of genomic imprinting. Transmission of the same
chromosomal deletion from the maternal side leads to Angelman syndrome, a disease
completely different from Prader-Willi syndrome.
Deletion of paternal origin of chromosome 15q11-13; is present in more than 400,000 patients
worldwide; three times more common in boys than girls.
Patients have low tone, ligamentous laxity, hip dysplasia, scoliosis, osteopenia, and childhood
obesity (OMIM #176270).50
Subtypes
Paternal deletions have a typical Prader-Willi syndrome phenotype.51
Uniparental maternal deletions have a milder subtype.51
Uniparental maternal deletion and a mosaic trisomy have a severe phenotype.51
Preoperative Workup
Metabolic laboratory studies should be obtained because of the high risk of diabetes mellitus.
Growth hormone treatment is useful in improving body composition but does not affect the
rate or severity of curves.52,53
Sleep studies are indicated to rule out sleep apnea.
Cardiac evaluation is necessary because of high rates of congenital heart disease. Cardiac
failure is one of the most common causes of mortality in patients with Prader-Willi
syndrome.51
Spinal Manifestations
Scoliosis is present in 30% to 90% of patients and may occur without underlying structural
abnormality or may be associated with congenital malformations.54-56
Serial spinal cast immobilization/bracing may help resolve or delay progression in a
considerable number of young children (<3 years) with a curve less than 50°.57-58
Scoliosis is more likely to occur in the lumbar or thoracolumbar spine and more likely to be
kyphotic, particularly in patients with a higher body mass index.55

Surgical Management
Patients with Prader-Willi syndrome and early-onset scoliosis have been treated successfully
via serial cast immobilization and growth-friendly surgery.
In one-third of patients, serial cast immobilization may be curative; in other patients, serial cast
immobilization may delay the timing of growth-friendly surgery.50
A high rate of complications, including rod fractures, has been reported in these patients.58
In addition, the surgeon should be careful if using magnetically controlled growing rods
because patients with Prader-Willi syndrome are more likely to be morbidly obese, which
would increase the distance between the actuator and the magnet, reducing its efficacy. In
addition, as patients gain weight, magnetically controlled growing rods may not be able to
generate adequate force to elongate the spine properly.50
The combination of soft bone, kyphosis, and early-onset scoliosis results in a high rate of
proximal and distal junctional kyphosis in these patients (17% to 31%).50,55,58,59 An extreme
example is found in a report of a spinal dislocation because of proximal junctional failure 1
week after posterior spine fusion.60 (Figure 4)

Etiology
A mutation in a MECP2 gene on the long arm of the X chromosome that results in a
progressive loss of milestones beginning at approximately age 6 months and occurs almost
exclusively in females
Associated with loss of skills and speech, stereotypic movements, growth retardation, seizures,
and microcephaly (OMIM #312750)61
Spinal Manifestations
Scoliosis is present in as many as 75% of patients and is increased in nonambulatory
patients.62
Patients who are ambulatory at age 10 years and who have only mild scoliosis are 86% less
likely to proceed to scoliosis greater than 60° compared with their counterparts.63
Scoliosis is increased in frequency and severity in patients with the p.Arg270* mutation.64
Preoperative Workup
Cardiac evaluation because of increased risk of prolonged QT interval and sudden death65
Nonsurgical Management
Intensive, individualized postural and motor activity programs may improve motor function.
These programs do not appear to alter the rate of progression of scoliosis66
Surgical Management
High rate of major medical complications, with as many as 63% experiencing pulmonary
complications and 37% experiencing gastrointestinal complications.67
Cohen et al68 reported higher rates of respiratory failure and longer intensive care unit stays
in patients with Rett syndrome compared with patients who had other etiologies of
neuromuscular scoliosis.
Down Syndrome
Etiology

Trisomy of all or part of chromosome 21.
Occurs in 1 in 600 to 800 live births.
Associated with increased maternal age (OMIM #190685)
Preoperative Workup
Cardiac disease in as many as 50% of patients, particularly atrioventricular septal defects69
(Resource 6)
Ten to 20 times increased risk of leukemia70
Increased risk of gastrointestinal malformations: stenosis, atresia, imperforate anus, and
Hirschsprung disease
Spinal Manifestations
Atlantoaxial instability is present in 9% to 31% of patients.
If the atlanto-dens interval is greater than 5 mm, high-risk activities should be limited.
If the atlanto-dens interval is greater than 10 mm or is associated with myelomalacia, spinal
fusion should be considered.71,72
Occipitoatlantal hypermobility is present in 8% to 71% of patients; however, it typically is
symptomatic in only 1.5%. Fusion is recommended if symptomatic or associated with
myelomalacia.71-74
Scoliosis is present in 9% of patients.69,71,72 Successful brace treatment has been reported in
several case series.75
Spondylolysis is present in as many as 18% of patients, and spondylolisthesis is present in as
many as 35% of patients.76
Surgical Management
Previous studies have reported a complication rate as high as 57% with the surgical
management of scoliosis. Multiple studies have reported high rates of pseudarthrosis, implant
failure, junctional failure, and loss of correction.75,77
High complication rates (33% to 73%) also are reported for instrumentation in the upper
cervical spine, with high rates of nonunion, loss of reduction, neurologic complications, and
CSF leaks.78,79 Postoperative immobilization with the use of a halo vest is recommended.

Osteogenesis Imperfecta
Etiology
Osteogenesis imperfecta is a disorder of congenital bone fragility.
To date, more than 19 different types are listed on the OMIM database, with new types
identified regularly.
Approximately 90% of cases are associated with abnormal type I collagen.
Spinal Manifestations
Spinal deformity in osteogenesis imperfecta is related to the severity of osseous
involvement.80-84 Anissipour et al80 evaluated the progression of scoliosis in a large cohort of
patients with various types of osteogenesis imperfecta and found the most rapid progression
in patients with type III osteogenesis imperfecta.
The morphology of the vertebral bodies in patients with osteogenesis imperfecta ranges from
normal contours to flattened, wedged, and biconcave; patients with biconcave vertebra are
more likely to have severe scoliosis.83,85,86

Spondylolysis is twice as common in patients with osteogenesis imperfecta compared with the
healthy pediatric population, and spondylolysis and spondylolisthesis are frequently
asymptomatic in this patient population. As many as 40% of patients may have pedicle
elongation, which can occur with or without pars fracture.87
Basilar invagination in patients with osteogenesis imperfecta ranges from platybasia to more
progressive forms that can result in paralysis. Overall, it primarily occurs in patients with more
severe involvement and kyphosis, particularly in those with type III osteogenesis imperfecta.88
Symptoms typically develop in early adolescence, and signs include headache, lower cranial
nerve problems, hyperreflexia, quadriparesis, ataxia, and nystagmus; however, many patients
remain asymptomatic89 (Resource 7).
Medical Management
Diphosphonate therapy helps improve bone quality for fixation and improves the bone pain
and overall quality of life.90,91
Pamidronate may help reverse some of the pathologic changes of the deformed bone and
may prevent scoliosis in some younger children.92-94
Surgical Management
Correcting curves in severely soft bone is difficult because the stability of fixation depends on
the strength of the bone and the quality of fixation purchase. Polymethyl methacrylate has
been used for additional fixation.95-97
Preoperative halo gravity traction or intraoperative halo traction with the use of multiple pins
may be useful; however, sixth and fourth cranial nerve palsies have been reported in patients
with osteogenesis imperfecta.98-100
Care must be taken with patient positioning for surgical treatment because of chest wall
deformities and joint contractures and to avoid fracture of fragile extremities and ribs.
Fatality has been reported from intraoperative rib fractures.101 (Figure 6)
Several recent large case series noted 50% major curve correction with minimal
complications, including proximal junctional kyphosis requiring revision in 2 of 30
patients.102,103

Arthrogryposis Multiplex Congenita
Etiology
Descriptive term encompassing more than 400 conditions with multiple inheritance patterns
Characterized by multiple nonprogressive congenital joint contractures
Present in 1 in 3,000 live births. May result from abnormal anterior horn cells104,105 (Resource
8).
Spinal Manifestations
Scoliosis is present in 2% to 69% of affected patients and is more likely to be rigid and severe
and progress after skeletal maturity. An increased rate of thoracic insufficiency is observed
because of weakened and fibrotic intercostal muscles and thoracic lordosis, resulting in
obstructive and restrictive pulmonary dysfunction.106,108
Three predominant curve types have been described: congenital, neuromuscular, and
idiopathic-like. The neuromuscular form occurs in approximately 30% of patients.
Amyoplasia is the most common form of arthrogryposis multiplex congenita
(AMC).108 Subsequent studies have found that the congenital form of scoliosis tends to be
associated with the syndromic type of AMC.106,108,109

Medical Management
Bracing is of limited utility in most patients with AMC, but it may be an effective delay tactic in
some patients and has been shown to prevent surgical treatment in ambulatory patients with
a curve of less than 30°.107,110
Surgical Management
Surgeons must evaluate patients for hip flexion contractures preoperatively because these
contractures may affect intraoperative positioning or the ability to sit postoperatively.110
Curves tend to be more severe and often are rigid, requiring preoperative traction or multiple
releases and osteotomies to adequately balance the spine.
Bruck Syndrome
Etiology
Bruck syndrome (multiple nonprogressive joint contractures present from birth) is a rare
autosomal recessive form of osteogenesis imperfecta in addition to AMC and occurs because
of a mutation in FKBP10 (OMIM #259450) or PLOD2 (OMIM #609220).
In addition to the multiple joint contractures, pterygia, and fractures, patients may have
scoliosis, kyphoscoliosis, cervical kyphosis or spondylolisthesis, severe limb deformity, and
short stature.111
Spinal Manifestations
Patients have multiple vertebral bone fractures. Scoliosis, kyphoscoliosis, cervical kyphosis, or
spondylolisthesis may develop.111

Fibrous Dysplasia
Etiology
Fibrous dysplasia results from a non-inherited somatic activating mutation of the GNAS gene
and may be monostotic (affecting one bone) or polyostotic (affecting multiple bones).112,113
The trio of polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, café-au-lait spots, and precocious puberty is referred
to as McCune-Albright syndrome and occurs because of an activating mutation of GNAS1 on
chromosome 20q13.32 (OMIM #174800).
Spinal Manifestations
Scoliosis is observed in 40% to 52% of patients with polyostotic fibrous dysplasia and is
associated with disease severity and leg-length discrepancy.114,115 (Figure 8)
Chiari malformations and basilar invagination may occur in 6% to 7% of patients with
craniofacial fibrous dysplasia.116

Increased blood loss has been reported in patients with McCune-Albright syndrome and has
been attributed to increased vascularity of the dysplastic bone and platelet dysfunction in
some patients; it may be reversed via platelet transfusions.117,118
Diphosphonates have been attempted and have not been found to be beneficial at preventing
the progression of scoliosis.114
Surgical Management
During preoperative planning, advanced imaging studies, such as positron emission
tomography or CT, should be considered to determine the extent of spinal involvement.
Studies on surgical treatment in patients with fibrous dysplasia and spinal involvement or
McCune-Albright syndrome are limited; however, management and outcomes appear to
correlate with the extent of spinal involvement. Patients with substantial spinal involvement
have an increased risk for implant failure and may require structural grafts or cement
augmentation.119

Larsen Syndrome
Etiology
Multiple etiologies have been reported; most associated with an autosomal dominant
mutation in Filamin B (OMIM #150250) or an autosomal recessive mutation in carbohydrate
sulfotransferase 3 (OMIM #245600).
The autosomal dominant form is associated with large joint dislocations, foot deformity, and
craniofacial abnormalities.129
The autosomal recessive form is associated with multiple joint dislocations, short stature,
and congenital heart abnormalities.
Preoperative Workup
Cardiac: aortic dilation, mitral valve prolapse
Anesthesia: increased rate of malignant hyperthermia, tracheomalacia, and hyperelastic rib
cage, which may result in respiratory failure
Spinal Manifestations
Cervical kyphosis: marked hypoplasia of cervical vertebra; frequently progressive; present in
infancy and may result in spondyloptosis of cervical vertebra, paralysis, and death.121
Kyphoscoliosis has been reported.122
Surgical Management
Dural ectasia and deficient anterior and posterior structures have been described.
Preoperative CT is recommended to better assess bony structures.
Anterior fusion alone is not recommended in very young patients. Posterior fusion alone has
been attempted and is associated with good early results; however, later anterior fusion
occasionally is required to attain adequate decompression and fusion, particularly in patients
with severe cervical kyphosis.121,123-125
Postoperative immobilization in a halo vest is recommended.125
